text: Two English tourists take a boat out to Almanzora, a small island off the Spanish coast, and find a fishing village with children in it and nobody else. The children watch them, and smile. Chicho Ibáñez Serrador spends 112 minutes on a situation a lesser thriller would burn through in thirty, and the slowness is the argument: the couple keep behaving like tourists, trying doors, asking after the adults, waiting for the ordinary explanation a holiday is entitled to. An island is a closed room with better weather. What the film watches most closely is the lag, the stretch of time in which two grown people go on refusing to read a place that has already made its decision about them. The dread is in the delay rather than in any reveal.

Bodyguard work is mostly standing still, and Johnnie To builds all eighty-four minutes of this out of that fact. A triad boss named Lung survives one attempt on his life and hires five men, Curtis, James, Mike, Roy and Shin, to see that there is not a second. They are strangers to one another, hired by the day, and the film cares far more about the arrangement than about the shooting: who takes which angle, who moves first, how much of a working relationship can form between men not supposed to have one. The premise is one line long, and nothing further is required of it. Long stretches are waiting. That is not a lull before the action, it is the action, held still. Eighty-four minutes leaves no room for a subplot, and none is missed.

A film about the hunt for a child murderer, made in Germany in 1958, can show almost nothing of the crime, and this one is content to be left with the man doing the looking. Ladislao Vajda gives him a hundred minutes and a reputation to spend. The detective starts the case respected and finishes somewhere else entirely, still working, still certain, well past the point where certainty does him any good. The ordinary furniture of a search is all here. What sits under it is a pressure the genre usually keeps offstage: a man who cannot put the case down and is aware that he cannot. A thriller wants a solution. Vajda keeps his attention on what wanting one has already taken from the person who wants it.

The crimes are small, too small for a plot to be built on them, and Tsai Ming-liang does not try. Four young people circulate through Taipei in 1993, crossing paths more often than any of them intends, and the film gives its attention to the intervals: the time it takes to eat, to follow someone, to sit in a room with the door shut. Nothing accumulates the way a crime story accumulates. What builds instead is proximity, in a city dense enough that strangers keep reappearing and indifferent enough that the reappearing settles nothing. A hundred and six minutes at that patience is a demand, and the right one. The loneliness here is never announced. It is measured out at actual length, which is the only honest way to show it.

Klaus lies in an iron lung, and the machine breathing for him has also fixed him in place, at the disposal of whoever happens to be in the room. That room, in Agustí Villaronga's 1986 film, holds a teenager named Ángelo, who has come to care for him. Klaus is German, a doctor, and carries a past the film does not have him narrate. A doctor is a person trained to keep others alive; here he is the one being kept. Two people, one house, 112 minutes. The horror is not an event but an arrangement, and the arrangement never needs forcing: a man who cannot leave, cannot be left, and takes every breath by the grace of someone he did not choose. What the film examines is care itself, and the fact that being tended and being controlled can look identical from outside the door.

A man steps into a telephone box on a public street to make a call, and afterwards the door will not open. Antonio Mercero has thirty-five minutes and one prop, and wastes neither. People stop. Someone tries the handle from outside, then someone else, and the trap inside the trap comes into view: a man behind glass in daylight, on a busy pavement, registers to everyone passing as an inconvenience rather than an emergency. Comedy and dread run on the same rail here and the film never has to pick one. Thirty-five minutes is exactly as long as a single idea can be held at full tension, and the idea is that a familiar piece of street furniture was always, technically, a box a person shuts himself into.

Villar del Río is a Castilian town, so when American officials are announced, the whole place puts on Andalusian costume. Luis García Berlanga's 1953 comedy watches a village rehearse itself into the Spain it assumes foreigners have already pictured: a flamenco performer brought in, the streets redecorated, the parts assigned. The Marshall Plan is the occasion; the joke points inward, at how quickly a place will agree to be an image of itself when there is money on the other side of the performance. Seventy-eight minutes, and the bulk of them are preparation, which makes this a comedy of waiting for a visit rather than a comedy of the visit. The costumes are funny. What the townspeople expect them to buy is not.

William Franklin comes back to Ireland in 1939 because his politics have cost him his job in America, and takes a post at St. Jude's, a school for wayward boys. He is the first teacher there who is not a cleric, and that single fact organizes everything after it. He has no standing inside the order that runs the place; Brother John, who has all of it, holds that boys are improved by strong discipline. Aisling Walsh keeps the ninety-four minutes almost entirely inside the building, so the disagreement cannot be conducted anywhere except in front of the children it concerns. The date is doing work too: a man who has already lost one job for what he thinks, walking into an institution where what he thinks is not currency.

Three thieves want the same piece of jade, and so does an internationally known professional whose luck is catastrophic. Between all of them and the stone stands a security chief obliged to be in several places at once, and Ning Hao's 2006 comedy runs almost wholly on the collisions this produces. The construction matters more than the theft. Ninety-eight minutes of plans failing into one another takes the sort of engineering a farce either has or does not, and the pleasure is in watching one man's solution turn into another man's disaster while the jade sits there, indifferent to all of it. Nobody here is competent enough to be cool. That is the choice that keeps it funny, and a heist film almost never makes it.

They hit the man on the bicycle with their car and drive on, because stopping would mean explaining who was in the car with whom. Juan Antonio Bardem's 1955 film lays that exchange rate out without comment: an affair is the fact that cannot survive daylight, and a body on a road is, by comparison, a thing that might be managed. The film is less interested in whether the two of them are caught than in the hours and the days afterwards, when nothing can be said and everything has to continue as before. Caimán's hundred of Spanish cinema keeps it, and the reason is not hard to locate at all. The distance between the people inside the car and the man on the road needs no line of dialogue; the car establishes it.

The rain will not stop, 1999 is running out, and a plumber has left a hole in one man's floor. Tsai Ming-liang surrounds that with a plague that has emptied most of Taiwan, which on paper makes this science fiction, and it behaves nothing like science fiction. The catastrophe stays at the edges, water everywhere, a building that will not dry, an island going quiet, while the film concentrates its ninety-five minutes on one floor, the man above it, the woman below it, and the fact that a hole works in both directions. It is an intrusion and it is the only contact available. Apocalypse is the wrong register for something this domestic: the end of the world arrives as a repair nobody is coming back to finish.

The band is assembled out of whoever in Hengchun is available, which turns out to be neither many people nor the right ones. Aga has come back to the town frustrated after singing elsewhere; Tomoko has been handed the job of producing a local warm-up act for a Japanese star's beach concert; five residents with no particular claim to a stage are recruited. Wei Te-sheng spends 129 minutes on this, long for a comedy about a poor band, and the length is where the film lives, in a small town's negotiations with Japan, with visitors, with its own sense of what it has to offer people who arrive expecting something. Taiwan sent it to the Academy Awards as its international submission. The concert is the errand. The town is the subject.

Yueh-chen cannot say it herself, so she sends Kerou to say it for her, and Shihao falls for the messenger. Yee Chih-yen's eighty-five minutes are built almost entirely from manoeuvres of that kind, the errands and proxies teenagers use to keep from stating anything in the first person. Kerou is left holding an attachment she did not ask for and cannot answer, and the film declines to hurry her toward an answer. The patience is the whole method. A modest high-school picture from 2002 sits on the Golden Horse hundred of Chinese-language films, which is not where a story with no crisis in it usually ends up: no lesson, no catastrophe, three young people at the age when not knowing is a condition rather than a stage.

A sabbatical is a year in which nothing is required to happen, and José Luis Cuerda built a comedy on precisely that. Teodoro teaches engineering in the United States and comes home to Spain with twelve empty months in front of him. No wedding to arrange, no inheritance, no crime: the apparatus a comedy normally leans on is simply absent, and 106 minutes have to be filled by other means. What the film has instead is the return itself, a man walking back into a country he left, obliged to occupy it rather than pass through. Comedy without a plot is a rarer contract than it sounds, since every minute has to be funny on its own account instead of borrowing credit from wherever the story was going.
